sections.heading: What does atrial fibrillation feel like?
sections.body:
The NHS lists an irregular pulse, palpitations, a fast heartbeat, tiredness and chest tightness among the main signs of atrial fibrillation. Breathlessness, dizziness and reduced ability to exercise are also listed. Sometimes there are no symptoms at all. In that case the condition may be found at a routine check-up or when tests are done for something else. In some cases it can be picked up by a pulse check.

NHS inform describes atrial fibrillation as not usually life threatening in itself. It adds that many people live normal healthy lives with the condition. The British Heart Foundation (BHF) likewise says there is no cure but people with AF can lead healthy lives.

sections.heading: What are the different types of atrial fibrillation?
sections.body:
NHS inform sorts atrial fibrillation into types by how long the episodes last. Paroxysmal AF comes and goes, with episodes lasting from minutes to hours. Persistent AF is when an episode lasts for more than seven days. Long-standing persistent AF is continuous for over a year. In permanent AF the heart rhythm does not go back to normal.

The BHF describes permanent AF as living with the condition long term, even after treatment. Paroxysmal AF can be hard to catch because the rhythm comes and goes. Royal Papworth Hospital describes paroxysmal AF as episodes that start and stop on their own. The NHS describes the condition as intermittent, persistent, long-term persistent or permanent.

sections.heading: How is atrial fibrillation diagnosed?
sections.body:
The NHS advises seeing a GP if a person thinks they may have symptoms. It also advises contacting the GP if palpitations keep happening or get worse, or if treatment is not helping. A pulse that is irregular, or very fast at rest, is also a reason to contact the GP. At the appointment the clinician asks about symptoms and checks the heart rate.

Diagnosis usually relies on an ECG, a recording of the heart's electrical activity. The NHS says an echocardiogram, a chest X-ray or blood tests may also be arranged. A portable ECG recorder can help diagnose paroxysmal AF, because it records the heart rate for 24 hours or longer.

sections.heading: What treatments are there for atrial fibrillation?
sections.body:
The NHS says there is currently no cure for atrial fibrillation, but treatment should help manage the symptoms and lower the risk of complications. Treatment aims to control the heart rate and rhythm and to reduce the risk of stroke. Medicines include beta blockers and anti-arrhythmic drugs. Anticoagulants, which are blood-thinning medicines, lower the risk of clots and stroke. A local NHS formulary says a vitamin K antagonist is offered if newer direct-acting oral anticoagulants are not suitable.

Some people have cardioversion, ablation or a pacemaker. NICE describes catheter ablation as an option when medicines fail or are not suitable. The usual catheter ablation techniques use radiofrequency energy or a cryoballoon. NHLBI says rhythm control may be used for people who have only recently started having AF, or for athletes and other highly active people. A UK charity leaflet advises that anticoagulation continues even after an apparently successful ablation.

sections.heading: How can people live with atrial fibrillation?
sections.body:
NHLBI lists weight control, limiting alcohol and stimulants that raise the heart rate, staying active, managing stress and eating heart-healthy foods. It says reaching a healthy weight can reduce how severe and how frequent episodes are. NHS inform also mentions limiting caffeine and alcohol, managing weight and exercising regularly.

The BHF says working out what triggers episodes is an important part of self-management. Its exercise guidance is that people with permanent AF can generally exercise if they feel well, while people with paroxysmal AF are advised to exercise only when in normal rhythm. NHLBI notes that blood thinners carry risks, including the possibility of severe bleeding in the brain. After an ablation, providers often want regular check-ups to look at healing and any new episodes.

sections.heading: Is atrial fibrillation serious, and when is it an emergency?
sections.body:
NHLBI says atrial fibrillation can lead to serious complications, especially if it is untreated or undiagnosed. The Stroke Association describes it as a condition that raises the risk of a serious stroke. A Heart Rhythm Alliance patient booklet describes the outlook for people with AF as excellent.

The NHS says to call 999 for a fast or irregular heartbeat together with chest pain, shortness of breath, fainting or confusion. It advises against driving yourself to A&E. For stroke signs such as a drooping face, weak arm or trouble speaking, the Stroke Association says to call 999 straight away. For symptoms that are not an emergency, the NHS advises seeing a GP. The Stroke Association says treatment often includes anticoagulants to lower the risk of clots and stroke.

faqs.a: The NHS says there is currently no cure for atrial fibrillation. Treatment should help manage the symptoms and lower the risk of complications. It aims to control the heart rate and rhythm and to reduce the risk of stroke. Options include medicines, anticoagulants and, in some cases, cardioversion or ablation.

NHS inform says atrial fibrillation is not usually life threatening in itself, and many people live normal healthy lives with it. However, NHLBI says it can lead to serious complications, especially if untreated or undiagnosed. The Stroke Association says it raises the risk of a serious stroke.

faqs.q: Can you have atrial fibrillation without symptoms?
faqs.a: Yes. The NHS says sometimes there are no symptoms. The condition may then be found at a routine check-up or during tests for something else. In some cases a pulse check can detect it, and an ECG is usually used to diagnose it.

faqs.q: What is the difference between paroxysmal and permanent AF?
faqs.a: NHS inform groups atrial fibrillation by how long episodes last. Paroxysmal AF comes and goes, with episodes lasting from minutes to hours. In permanent AF the rhythm does not return to normal. Persistent AF lasts longer than seven days, and long-standing persistent AF is continuous for over a year.

faqs.q: What lifestyle changes help with atrial fibrillation?
faqs.a: NHLBI lists weight control, limiting alcohol and stimulants that raise the heart rate, staying active, managing stress and eating heart-healthy foods. It says reaching a healthy weight can reduce how severe and how frequent episodes are. NHS inform also mentions limiting caffeine.

faqs.q: When should someone call 999 about a fast or irregular heartbeat?
faqs.a: The NHS says to call 999 for a fast or irregular heartbeat together with chest pain, shortness of breath, fainting or confusion. It advises against driving yourself to A&E. For milder or repeated palpitations, it advises seeing a GP. A pulse that is irregular, or very fast at rest, is also a reason to contact the GP.
